content: Bunium persicum, commonly known as black cumin, is a plant belonging to the Apiaceae family. The dried fruits of Bunium persicum are utilized as a culinary spice in regions such as Northern India, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Iran. Locally, it is referred to as kala jeera (meaning black cumin) or shahi jeera (meaning imperial cumin) in Hindi, zireh kuhi (meaning wild cumin) in Persian, and siyoh dona (meaning black seed) in Tajiki. Outside these regions, the spice is virtually unknown and should not be confused with Nigella sativa, which is also often called black cumin. In Bengali, kalo jeera refers to Nigella sativa, not Bunium persicum, and Nigella is widely used in Bengali cuisine, whereas Bunium persicum is rare. The plant grows wild across a broad geographical range, from southeastern Europe to southern Asia. It typically reaches a height of about 60 cm and a width of 25 cm, featuring finely divided leaves and hermaphroditic flowers that are pollinated by insects and are self-fertile. The small, rounded taproot of the plant is edible, either raw or cooked, and is said to have a flavor reminiscent of sweet chestnuts. The leaves can be used as a herb or garnish, similar to parsley. There is some debate among experts as to whether Bunium persicum is the same species as Bunium bulbocastanum, as both share similar characteristics and uses. Medicinal Applications of Black Cumin The fruit of Bunium persicum is a rich source of thymol, a compound with significant medicinal properties. Thymol is used as an anthelmintic to treat hookworm infections and as an antiseptic in various proprietary formulations. It also acts as a stimulant, promoting increased secretion and discharge of urine, alleviating flatulence, enhancing stomach function, and arresting bleeding. Digestive Disorders Cumin seeds are highly effective in managing digestive disorders such as biliousness, morning sickness, indigestion, atonic dyspepsia, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome, and flatulent colic. A decoction can be prepared by boiling one teaspoon of cumin seeds in a glass of water, mixing it with one teaspoon of fresh coriander leaf juice and a pinch of salt. This preparation can be consumed twice daily after meals to treat diarrhea. Piles/Hemorrhoids Black cumin is beneficial in the treatment of piles or hemorrhoids. A mixture of 60 grams of cumin seeds, half of which are roasted, is ground into a fine powder. Three grams of this powder can be taken with water for relief. Insomnia Cumin is valuable in alleviating sleeplessness. A teaspoon of fried cumin seed powder mixed with the pulp of a ripe banana can be consumed at night to induce sleep. Renal Colic A mixture of black cumin seeds, caraway seeds, and black salt is effective in managing renal colic. About 20 grams of cumin seeds, 12 grams of caraway seeds, and 6 grams of black salt are ground together and mixed with a small amount of vinegar. This preparation can be taken in doses of 3 grams every hour until relief is achieved. Common Cold Diluted cumin water serves as an antiseptic beverage and is highly beneficial in treating common colds and fevers. To prepare cumin water, a teaspoon of cumin is added to boiling water, simmered briefly, and then allowed to cool. For colds associated with a sore throat, small pieces of dry ginger can be added to the water to soothe throat irritation. Breast Milk Secretion A decoction of cumin seeds mixed with milk and honey, taken once daily throughout pregnancy, supports the healthy development of the fetus, facilitates childbirth, and enhances breast milk secretion. Amnesia Cumin seeds are valuable in treating amnesia or memory dullness. A mixture of 3 grams of black cumin seeds and 12 grams of pure honey can be consumed to alleviate this condition. Boils A paste made from black cumin seeds ground in water can be applied to boils for beneficial results. Scorpion Stings A paste of cumin seeds prepared with onion juice can be applied to scorpion stings to reduce the frequency of painful sensations. Culinary and Other Uses Cumin seeds are extensively used in mixed spices and for flavoring curries, soups, sausages, bread, and cakes. They are a key ingredient in curry powders, pickles, and chutneys. In Indian medicine, cumin is also used as a carminative. Use in Medicine Nigella sativa, another plant often referred to as black cumin, has been used medicinally for centuries in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. It has been traditionally employed to address respiratory health, gastrointestinal health, kidney and liver function, circulatory and immune system support, and general well-being. In Islamic tradition, it is considered one of the most potent healing remedies, with Prophet Muhammad reportedly stating that black seed can cure every disease except death. Ibn Sina, a renowned physician, described Nigella as a seed that stimulates energy and aids recovery from fatigue and despondency. It is also included in the Medicine of the Prophet (Tibb-e-Nabavi) as a natural remedy for numerous ailments. In the Unani Tibb system of medicine, Nigella sativa is regarded as a valuable treatment for various diseases. The seeds have been traditionally used in the Middle East and Southeast Asia to treat conditions such as asthma, bronchitis, rheumatism, and related inflammatory diseases. They are also used to enhance milk production in nursing mothers, promote digestion, and combat parasitic infections. The oil derived from Nigella sativa has been applied to treat skin conditions like eczema and boils, as well as to alleviate cold symptoms. Its diverse applications have earned it the Arabic title Habbatul Barakah, meaning the seed of blessing.
